--- title: | Unsupervised \ Machine Learning jupyter: python3 format: revealjs: scrollable: true navigation-mode: vertical controls-layout: bottom-right controls-tutorial: true incremental: false theme: [default, styles.scss] execute: echo: true eval: true warning: false revealjs-plugins: - pointer - verticator filters: - code-fullscreen - reveal-auto-agenda editor: source draft: true order: 15 date: 12-01-26 description: An introduction to unsupervized machine learning. --- # Unsupervised Machine Learning ## Supervised Machine Learning Supervised learning uses features and a known outcome: $$ \boldsymbol X = (X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)\mrTr $$ where $$ X_i = (x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \ldots, x_{ip}) $$ and $$ \boldsymbol Y = (Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_n)\mrTr. $$ The outcome $Y_i$ guides the model during training. ## Unsupervised Machine Learning Unsupervised learning uses the feature matrix without a known outcome: $$ \boldsymbol X = (X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)\mrTr, $$ where each observation contains $p$ features: $$ X_i = (x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \ldots, x_{ip}). $$ Clustering searches for groups whose members are more similar to one another than to members of other groups. ## Questions Clustering Can Answer - Which observations have similar feature values? - Are there compact groups, curved groups, or regions of high density? - Which observations do not fit any group? - Does a useful grouping appear at more than one level of detail? Cluster labels describe structure in the available features. They do not automatically represent meaningful real-world categories. ## Feature Scaling Distance-based algorithms can give variables with large numerical ranges too much influence. ::: {#a446704f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # General scaling template scaler = StandardScaler() X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_blobs) ``` ::: Standardization gives each feature a mean near 0 and a standard deviation near 1. Fit the scaler on training data before transforming new data in a production workflow. ## Datasets Used in the Examples {.smaller} ::: {#58906f50 .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='5.2' layout-ncol='2' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} cluster_plot( X_blobs, blob_truth, "Compact clusters", ) cluster_plot( X_moons, moon_truth, "Curved clusters", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: The known groups appear only to explain the synthetic examples. The clustering models do not receive these labels. ## Principal Component Analysis Principal component analysis (PCA) creates new, uncorrelated variables called principal components. - The first component captures the largest possible amount of variation. - Each later component captures the largest remaining variation while staying perpendicular to earlier components. - PCA supports visualization, compression, and preprocessing. - PCA does not assign observations to clusters. ## PCA Template {.smaller} ::: {#0d241e06 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} pca = PCA(n_components=2) X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_blobs) pca_data = pd.DataFrame( X_pca, columns=["PC1", "PC2"], ).assign(group=pd.Categorical(blob_truth.astype(str))) ( ggplot(pca_data, aes("PC1", "PC2", color="group")) + geom_point(alpha=0.75, size=2) + scale_color_brewer(type="qual", palette="Dark2") + labs( title="Two-dimensional PCA representation", color="Known group", ) + theme_minimal() + theme(figure_size=(6.4, 3.8)) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-5-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: # Clustering Techniques ## Major Clustering Families | Family | Definition of a cluster | Examples | |---|---|---| | Centroid based | Points near a common center | K-means, MiniBatch K-means | | Hierarchical | Points joined through a nested sequence | Agglomerative clustering, BIRCH | | Density based | Points in connected dense regions | DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, OPTICS | | Graph based | Points connected strongly in a similarity graph | Spectral clustering, affinity propagation | | Probabilistic | Points generated by a shared probability distribution | Gaussian mixture models | ## K-Means Clustering K-means assigns each observation to the nearest cluster center and updates the centers until the assignments stabilize. The algorithm minimizes the within-cluster sum of squares: $$ \sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{x_i \in C_k} \lVert x_i-\mu_k \rVert^2. $$ K-means works best for compact clusters of comparable size. You must choose $K$ before fitting the model. ## K-Means Template {.smaller} ::: {#a4f8e96b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} kmeans = KMeans( n_clusters=3, n_init="auto", random_state=42, ) kmeans_labels = kmeans.fit_predict(X_blobs) kmeans.cluster_centers_ cluster_plot( X_blobs, kmeans_labels, "K-means clustering", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: Use `predict()` to assign new observations to the fitted centers. ## Choosing the Number of K-Means Clusters {.smaller} ::: {#7bd22aa5 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} k_results = [] for k in range(2, 9): model = KMeans( n_clusters=k, n_init="auto", random_state=42, ) labels = model.fit_predict(X_blobs) k_results.append( { "k": k, "silhouette": silhouette_score(X_blobs, labels), } ) k_results = pd.DataFrame(k_results) ( ggplot(k_results, aes("k", "silhouette")) + geom_line(color="#0072B2", size=1) + geom_point(color="#0072B2", size=3) + labs( title="Silhouette score by number of clusters", x="Number of clusters", y="Silhouette score", ) + theme_minimal() + theme(figure_size=(6.4, 3.8)) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-7-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: Prefer a larger silhouette score, then check whether the grouping makes sense for the problem. ## MiniBatch K-Means Template {.smaller} MiniBatch K-means updates cluster centers from small batches rather than the full dataset. It usually runs faster on large datasets, with a possible loss in cluster quality. ::: {#615e1813 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} mini_batch = MiniBatchKMeans( n_clusters=3, batch_size=256, n_init="auto", random_state=42, ) mini_batch_labels = mini_batch.fit_predict(X_large) cluster_plot( X_large, mini_batch_labels, "MiniBatch K-means clustering", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-8-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: ## Bisecting K-Means Template {.smaller} Bisecting K-means repeatedly splits an existing cluster into two. This produces a hierarchy while retaining the speed and center-based interpretation of K-means. ::: {#806ced0a .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} bisecting = BisectingKMeans( n_clusters=3, random_state=42, ) bisecting_labels = bisecting.fit_predict(X_blobs) cluster_plot( X_blobs, bisecting_labels, "Bisecting K-means clustering", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: ## Hierarchical Clustering Hierarchical methods form nested clusters. - **Agglomerative methods** begin with one cluster per observation and merge clusters. - **Divisive methods** begin with one cluster and split it. - A dendrogram can show possible partitions at several levels. - Linkage determines how the method measures distance between clusters. `AgglomerativeClustering` provides Ward, complete, average, and single linkage. ## Agglomerative Clustering Template {.smaller} ::: {#b08c1011 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} agglomerative = AgglomerativeClustering( n_clusters=3, linkage="ward", ) agglomerative_labels = agglomerative.fit_predict(X_blobs) cluster_plot( X_blobs, agglomerative_labels, "Agglomerative clustering", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-10-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: Ward linkage minimizes the increase in within-cluster variance. Other linkages can use non-Euclidean distance metrics. ## Gaussian Mixture Models A Gaussian mixture model assumes that several Gaussian distributions generated the data. - Each component has its own mean and covariance structure. - `predict()` produces a cluster assignment. - `predict_proba()` produces the probability that an observation belongs to each component. - Full covariance matrices can represent elliptical clusters. The Bayesian information criterion (BIC) can help compare models with different numbers of components. ## Gaussian Mixture Template {.smaller} ::: {#0173b658 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} gmm = GaussianMixture( n_components=3, covariance_type="full", random_state=42, ) gmm.fit(X_elliptical) gmm_labels = gmm.predict(X_elliptical) membership_probabilities = gmm.predict_proba(X_elliptical) cluster_plot( X_elliptical, gmm_labels, "Gaussian mixture model", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-11-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: # Density and Graph Methods ## Density-Based Clustering Density-based methods search for connected regions containing many nearby observations. - They can recover clusters with curved or irregular boundaries. - They can mark isolated observations as noise with label `-1`. - They do not require spherical clusters. - Their tuning parameters describe neighborhood size or cluster persistence. These methods often work better than K-means when groups have irregular shapes. ## DBSCAN Template {.smaller} DBSCAN links core observations that have at least `min_samples` observations within distance `eps`. ::: {#17e76e71 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} dbscan = DBSCAN( eps=0.25, min_samples=8, ) dbscan_labels = dbscan.fit_predict(X_moons) cluster_plot( X_moons, dbscan_labels, "DBSCAN clustering", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-12-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: A small `eps` may label many observations as noise. A large `eps` may merge separate groups. ## HDBSCAN Template {.smaller} HDBSCAN examines cluster structure across several density levels. It can handle groups with different densities more effectively than one global DBSCAN radius. ::: {#5cce8d43 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} hdbscan = HDBSCAN( min_cluster_size=30, min_samples=10, copy=True, ) hdbscan_labels = hdbscan.fit_predict(X_moons) cluster_plot( X_moons, hdbscan_labels, "HDBSCAN clustering", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-13-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: `min_cluster_size` controls the smallest group the algorithm will retain. ## OPTICS Template {.smaller} OPTICS orders observations by reachability. This exposes density structure without committing to one neighborhood radius before fitting. ::: {#b0574df9 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} optics = OPTICS( min_samples=10, xi=0.10, min_cluster_size=0.10, ) optics_labels = optics.fit_predict(X_moons) cluster_plot( X_moons, optics_labels, "OPTICS clustering", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-14-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: `xi` controls how sharply the reachability plot must change to separate clusters. ## Spectral Clustering Template {.smaller} Spectral clustering builds a graph of nearby observations, embeds that graph, and clusters the embedding. It works well when groups are connected but not compact. ::: {#3f280d14 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} spectral = SpectralClustering( n_clusters=2, affinity="nearest_neighbors", n_neighbors=12, assign_labels="kmeans", random_state=42, ) spectral_labels = spectral.fit_predict(X_moons) cluster_plot( X_moons, spectral_labels, "Spectral clustering", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-15-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: Spectral clustering can become expensive as the number of observations grows. ## Mean Shift Template {.smaller} Mean shift moves observations toward local peaks in the estimated density. The fitted peaks serve as cluster centers. ::: {#4928f4f3 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} bandwidth = estimate_bandwidth( X_blobs, quantile=0.25, n_samples=300, ) mean_shift = MeanShift( bandwidth=bandwidth, bin_seeding=True, ) mean_shift_labels = mean_shift.fit_predict(X_blobs) cluster_plot( X_blobs, mean_shift_labels, "Mean shift clustering", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-16-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: Bandwidth strongly affects the number of detected clusters. ## BIRCH Template {.smaller} BIRCH incrementally summarizes observations in a clustering feature tree. It supports large datasets and can process data in batches. ::: {#09245629 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} birch = Birch( threshold=0.35, branching_factor=50, n_clusters=3, ) birch_labels = birch.fit_predict(X_large) cluster_plot( X_large, birch_labels, "BIRCH clustering", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-17-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: The threshold controls the radius of the subclusters stored in the tree. ## Affinity Propagation Template {.smaller} Affinity propagation passes messages between observations and selects representative observations called exemplars. The algorithm estimates the number of clusters from the data. ::: {#4d159ebf .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} affinity = AffinityPropagation( damping=0.80, preference=-20, random_state=42, ) affinity_labels = affinity.fit_predict(X_blobs) cluster_plot( X_blobs, affinity_labels, "Affinity propagation", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ![](15a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-18-output-1.png){width=614 height=365} ::: ::: The preference value influences how many exemplars the model selects. # Selecting and Evaluating a Model ## Comparison of Clustering Techniques {.smaller} | Technique | Must choose cluster count? | Irregular shapes? | Identifies noise? | Best use | |---|:---:|:---:|:---:|---| | K-means | Yes | No | No | Compact, similarly sized groups | | Agglomerative | Usually | Sometimes | No | Nested structure and smaller datasets | | Gaussian mixture | Yes | Elliptical | No | Probabilistic membership | | DBSCAN | No | Yes | Yes | Similar-density groups with noise | | HDBSCAN | No | Yes | Yes | Groups with varying density | | OPTICS | No | Yes | Yes | Exploring several density levels | | Spectral | Yes | Yes | No | Connected, nonlinear groups | | Mean shift | No | Sometimes | Optional | Density peaks in moderate datasets | | BIRCH | Optional | Limited | No | Large datasets and streaming batches | | Affinity propagation | No | Limited | No | Exemplar-based clusters in smaller datasets | ## Internal Evaluation Measures When no correct labels exist, internal measures compare compactness and separation. | Measure | Preferred value | Main idea | |---|---:|---| | Silhouette score | Larger, up to 1 | Compares within-cluster and nearest-cluster distances | | Davies-Bouldin index | Smaller, at least 0 | Compares within-cluster spread with separation | | Calinski-Harabasz score | Larger | Ratio of between-cluster to within-cluster variation | Metrics can favor simple geometric groups. Also inspect stability, domain meaning, and sensitivity to tuning choices. ## Evaluation Template ::: {#f37da2bd .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} evaluation = pd.DataFrame( { "measure": [ "Silhouette", "Davies-Bouldin", "Calinski-Harabasz", ], "value": [ silhouette_score(X_blobs, kmeans_labels), davies_bouldin_score(X_blobs, kmeans_labels), calinski_harabasz_score(X_blobs, kmeans_labels), ], } ) evaluation ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ```{=html}
measure value
0 Silhouette 0.760352
1 Davies-Bouldin 0.331706
2 Calinski-Harabasz 2378.207866
``` ::: ::: Remove observations labeled `-1` before computing these measures for a density-based model. ## General Clustering Workflow 1. Select features that represent meaningful similarity. 2. Handle missing values and standardize features when the method uses distance. 3. Plot a low-dimensional view while remembering that it may hide structure. 4. Fit several suitable algorithms and tuning values. 5. Compare internal measures, stability, and practical usefulness. 6. Document how new observations will receive labels, if prediction is required. Some clustering estimators support `predict()`. Others only assign labels to the observations used during fitting. ## Scikit-Learn Documentation - [Clustering](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html) - [Gaussian mixture models](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html) - [Decomposition and PCA](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/decomposition.html) - [Clustering performance evaluation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#clustering-performance-evaluation) The examples use the estimator pattern found throughout scikit-learn: ```python model = Estimator(...) labels = model.fit_predict(X) ``` ## Other Unsupervised Techniques in Scikit-Learn {.smaller} | Technique | Purpose | Example estimators | |---|---|---| | Manifold learning | Nonlinear low-dimensional representations | `TSNE`, `Isomap`, `MDS`, `LocallyLinearEmbedding` | | Matrix decomposition | Components, sources, or topics | `NMF`, `FastICA`, `DictionaryLearning`, `LatentDirichletAllocation` | | Anomaly detection | Unusual observations or novel cases | `IsolationForest`, `LocalOutlierFactor`, `OneClassSVM` | | Density estimation | Estimate an unknown probability density | `KernelDensity` | | Biclustering | Cluster rows and columns together | `SpectralCoclustering`, `SpectralBiclustering` | | Covariance estimation | Estimate feature dependence robustly | `LedoitWolf`, `MinCovDet`, `GraphicalLasso` | PCA and the clustering methods from this lecture represent only part of scikit-learn's unsupervised learning toolkit.
